    locate  ->  entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "..."
    impact  ->  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X   (one shot: callers, callees, type consumers, data flow, co-change, siblings)
    callers ->  entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in

## Project Overview

DevDesk is a terminal-based TUI (Text User Interface) application built with Go and Bubble Tea framework. It provides DevSecOps functionality including:
- System status monitoring (HTTP/HTTPS, ICMP, DNS, SSL checks)
- GitLab integration (authentication, project explorer, multi-select clone)
- Security scanning (Trivy CVE/secret/license/misconfig + Gitleaks secrets)
- Container management with real-time metrics, on Docker or Podman (`app.container_engine`)
- OCI resource management (image scanning, container launching, network inspection)
- Network diagnostics (DNS, route, ICMP, TCP, TLS, HTTP) + real-time port monitoring + this machine's interfaces + local port forwarding (unprivileged, loopback only) + a path trace under Diagnostics (Trace Path button, or `H` on the route row; no separate tab since DEVDESK-471) (native path trace, native Linux and WSL2 only: on macOS, Windows and WSL1 the button, `H`, `enter` and `ctrl+o` are greyed and the footer says why, DEVDESK-334; the column starts with this machine, its interface and its gateway; `ctrl+o` can start it from a running Docker Engine container instead (container and network rows, hops still traced from this machine); `H` on the Diagnostics route row opens the trace level on that host without starting it (greyed with the reason on an unsupported platform or a target the trace refuses), and in the trace level `enter` starts or restarts it, `ctrl+o` picks the source, `esc` cancels then goes back where it came from; under WSL2 the source row says `WSL2 (VM), not the Windows host` with the networking mode, and in NAT mode the gateway and TTL 1 hop are tagged `Windows host (virtual switch)` only when proven, DEVDESK-333; the interface row says `no route` when the kernel proves there is none and `undetermined` when the routing table could not be read, a no-route error keeps the local rows, a trace that ends on the hop limit or the deadline folds its silent tail into one `silent` row and marks the `last to answer` hop, and the target refuses a `:port`, DEVDESK-335)
- Multi-context configuration management via YAML
- Local workspaces management with git metadata
- Claude Code session list (`:agent-usage` / `:au`): sessions found on this machine, by project and date, and per session the agent tree (orchestrator and sub-agents: types, models, tokens, share of the total; sortable by Total; also per agent a state (running / idle / done / unknown, idle after 5 min without a transcript line) shown as a status dot in the first column (the `running` dot blinks, DEVDESK-151) and as text, tool calls and duration; and an indicative cost per agent, `Est. cost` (orange from 75 % and red from 90 % of the session's estimated cost, when at least two agents are priced), from prices you write in the context YAML (`agent_usage.prices`, none shipped), with the session's `Billed` cost and `Unattributed` in the header, DEVDESK-47; a `Breakdown` colour bar per agent and, with `tab` inside a session, a Breakdown tab splitting the whole session's tokens by category, model and agent, as a percentage of tokens, DEVDESK-98). An open session updates live: read again every 2 s while active, only what was appended; paused after 5 min with no write and no unfinished sub-agent, when its transcript is gone, or while the terminal is not focused (header `Updates › paused`, then `paused (terminal not focused)`; `app.when_unfocused: run` keeps it live); `ctrl+r` reads it again in full. ### Credentials Management

No secret DevDesk holds is written to a file DevDesk owns. `internal/credentials`
implements the `Storage` interface three ways and `Select()` picks exactly one —
writing to several at once is what let the old "secure" option store a token in
the credential manager *and* in plaintext:

| Storage | Backend | Notes |
|---------|---------|-------|
| `KeyringStorage` | Windows Credential Manager / macOS Keychain / Secret Service | via `zalando/go-keyring`, no cgo. The default. |
| `GitCredentialStorage` | git's configured credential helper | Only when the helper is not `store`, which writes plaintext. Context-aware. |
| `MemoryStorage` | this process | Last resort, and deliberately worse: the auth view says nothing was saved. |

`Select(context, preference)` returns a `Selection{Storage, Backend, Detail}`.
The order is keyring → git credential → memory; `app.secret_backend` in the
context config pins the head of it (`auto`, `keyring`, `git-credential`). A
pinned backend that is unreachable falls through to memory rather than silently
to the other one.

The router resolves one `Selection` per context and keeps it in
`shared.State.Secrets`. It must be reused for the lifetime of the context — a
second `Select()` call yields a fresh `MemoryStorage` that cannot see what the
first one holds.

`MigrateLegacySecrets` runs at startup and on every context switch: a
`gitlab.token` or `registry.password` left in a context file by an older build
is moved into the store and deleted from the YAML, with the result reported in
the auth view.

## Testing

Test files follow Go conventions (`*_test.go`):
- `internal/command/parser_test.go` - Command parser tests

Use table-driven tests where appropriate.

**`go test` does not detect races or explore fuzz targets.** `mise run test` runs
only the fuzz seeds, so `internal/agentusage` concurrency tests
(`TestConcurrent*`) need `mise run test-race`. To explore `FuzzIncrementalMatchesFull`
run `go test -fuzz=FuzzIncrementalMatchesFull -fuzztime=60s ./internal/agentusage`.

**HOME is shared across a test process.** `TestMain` in `internal/app` sets
`HOME` once for the whole process, so under `go test -count=N` a test finds
the files its own previous run wrote (context config, forge index cache), and
it fails from `-count=2` while `-count=1` passes (DEVDESK-36). A test that
writes under HOME isolates it with `t.Setenv("HOME", t.TempDir())` and
`USERPROFILE` too; in `internal/app`, call `isolateHome(t)` from
`harness_test.go` (already done by `routerAt`). `internal/ui/setup` is fixed
(DEVDESK-38): its `isolateHome(t)` helper in `model_test.go` is called by the
tests that write under HOME. Other packages whose TestMain does
`os.Setenv("HOME", …)` may have the same default. To find them:
`grep -rn 'os.Setenv("HOME"' --include=*_test.go`, then `go test -count=2` on each package.

**Never get a "free" port by `net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0")`, reading the
port, then `Close()`, and letting the code under test bind it later.** Between
the close and the bind, any `bind(0)` can be handed that very port: an
`httptest.NewServer` in the same test, another test, another process on the
runner. The symptom is an intermittent `address already in use`, mostly in CI
(Linux gave the just-closed port back to about 1 `bind(0)` in 7,000; DEVDESK-35,
D85 in `docs/backlog.md`).

- If the code under test takes a port, call `loopback.ReservePort(t)`
  (`internal/testutil/loopback`). On Linux it holds a socket bound with
  `SO_REUSEADDR`, never listening, until `t.Cleanup`: `bind(0)` and `connect()`
  cannot take the port, but `net.Listen` can.
- Otherwise let the server bind `:0` and read the real port, or keep the
  listener open and hand it to the code under test.
- Off Linux, `ReservePort` keeps the old behavior and the window stays open
  (on Windows Go does not set `SO_REUSEADDR`). That is known, not a local bug.
- `internal/testutil/loopback` is imported from `_test.go` files only; nothing
  enforces it yet.

**Test input and colour (DEVDESK-199).** Build keys only through
`internal/ui/testutil` (`Key`, `Keys`, `Type`, `Paste`, `Text`, `IsText`), never a
literal `tea.KeyPressMsg` or `tea.Key*`. `Key` returns a
`tea.KeyPressMsg` (`Keys` and `Type` return a message list), `Paste` a `tea.PasteMsg`; `Key` is strict: an unknown name
panics. The space key is built as a key (`Key("space")`), never matched through
`String()` (v1 `" "`, v2 `"space"`). Lip Gloss v2 has no global colour profile (`Style.Render` always emits full
colour), so a test needs no setup to check styling; it reads the SGR or strips it
with `ansi.Strip`. `internal/ui/testutil/source_guard_test.go` fails the suite on a
hand-built key, a `colorprofile` import outside `internal/app/profile_test.go` and
`internal/app/redraw_measure_test.go` or `SetColorProfile` in any `_test.go`. Paste tests
(`internal/app/paste_test.go`, `wrapped_input_test.go`, `component_form_test.go`):
a paste reaches the focused field, newlines become spaces in single-line fields,
and no key action fires (Rule 111).

**Space and key API (DEVDESK-200).** Production code matches the space key as

**Rule 122** — `Cell` returns plain text (it gets measured), color goes through `Style`. A `style.Render(...)` inside `Cell` gets truncated in the middle of its escape sequence and bleeds onto every following row.

**Rule 128** — A footer message goes through `components.FooterMessage`: three levels (neutral info, orange warning, red error), always centered, a single implementation. **Rule 139** — A `datatable`'s body is always `m.table.View()`, never a loading screen or a message: an empty table (loading, nothing to list, a filter with no results) stays a table — a header, no rows. The count goes in `GetHeaderInfo`, the status in the footer.

**Rule 129** — All UI text and all logs in **English US**.

**Rule 140** — An invalid form field is underlined through `theme.StyleInvalidField` (the only entry point to the underline API), and the error is also in the footer at level Error, derived on every render. The underline is never the only carrier.

**Rule 133** — `bubbles/textarea` is forbidden. Use `components.WrappedInput` for any multi-line text field.

- hookify-help: Get help with the hookify system
- hookify-list: List all configured hookify rules

- loop-start: Start a managed autonomous loop pattern with safety defaults and explicit stop conditions.
- loop-status: Inspect active loop state, progress, failure signals, and recommended intervention.
- marketing-campaign: Plan and execute a full marketing campaign. Accepts a product brief and returns positioning, landing page copy, email sequence, social posts, ad variants, video scripts, and a content calendar. Can also review existing copy for conversion quality.
- model-route: Recommend the best model tier for the current task based on complexity, risk, and budget.
- multi-backend: Run a backend-focused multi-model workflow for APIs, algorithms, data, and business logic.
- multi-execute: Execute a multi-model implementation plan while preserving Claude as the only filesystem writer.
- multi-frontend: Run a frontend-focused multi-model workflow for components, layouts, animation, and UI polish.
- multi-plan: Create a multi-model implementation plan without modifying production code.
- multi-workflow: Run a full multi-model development workflow with research, planning, execution, optimization, and review.
- orch-add-feature: Orchestrate building a brand-new feature end to end — research, plan, TDD, review, gated commit. Wrapper that kicks off the orch-add-feature skill.
- orch-build-mvp: Orchestrate bootstrapping a working MVP from a design/spec doc — ingest, slice, scaffold, TDD, review, gated commit (reuses the GAN harness). Wrapper for the orch-build-mvp skill.
- orch-change-feature: Orchestrate altering an existing, working feature to new desired behavior — update tests to the new spec, change impl, review, gated commit. Wrapper for the orch-change-feature skill.
- orch-fix-defect: Orchestrate fixing a bug — reproduce it as a failing regression test, fix to green, review, gated commit. Wrapper for the orch-fix-defect skill.
- orch-refine-code: Orchestrate a behavior-preserving refactor — confirm tests green, restructure without changing behavior, keep green, review, gated commit. Wrapper for the orch-refine-code skill.
- orch-review: Run the orch-review native Workflow over a diff (local changes or a GitHub PR) and report blocking vs advisory findings. Surface for the orch-review workflow.
- plan: Restate requirements, assess risks, and create step-by-step implementation plan. WAIT for user CONFIRM before touching any code.
- plan-canvas: Open a plan or HTML artifact in the browser Plan Canvas for annotate-and-approve review
- plan-prd: Generate a lean, problem-first PRD and hand off to /plan for implementation planning.
- pm2: Analyze a project and generate PM2 service commands for detected frontend, backend, or database services.
- pr: Create a GitHub PR from current branch with unpushed commits — discovers templates, analyzes changes, pushes
- project-init: Detect a project's stack and produce a dry-run ECC onboarding plan using the repository's install manifests and stack mappings.
- projects: List known projects and their instinct statistics
- promote: Promote project-scoped instincts to global scope
- prp-commit: Quick commit with natural language file targeting — describe what to commit in plain English
- prp-implement: Execute an implementation plan with rigorous validation loops
- prp-plan: Create comprehensive feature implementation plan with codebase analysis and pattern extraction
- prp-pr: Create a GitHub PR from current branch with unpushed commits — discovers templates, analyzes changes, pushes
- prp-prd: Interactive PRD generator - problem-first, hypothesis-driven product spec with back-and-forth questioning
- prune: Delete pending instincts older than 30 days that were never promoted
- python-review: Comprehensive Python code review for PEP 8 compliance, type hints, security, and Pythonic idioms. Invokes the python-reviewer agent.
- quality-gate: Run the ECC formatter quality gate for a single file and report remediation steps.
- react-build: Fix React build failures (Vite, webpack, Next.js, CRA, Parcel, esbuild, Bun) incrementally — JSX/TSX compile errors, hydration mismatches, server/client component boundary failures, missing types. Invokes the react-build-resolver agent for minimal, surgical fixes.
- react-review: Comprehensive React/JSX code review for hook correctness, render performance, server/client component boundaries, accessibility, and React-specific security. Invokes the react-reviewer agent (and typescript-reviewer alongside on TSX/JSX changes).
- react-test: Enforce TDD workflow for React. Write React Testing Library tests first (behavior-focused, accessibility-first), then implement components. Detects Vitest or Jest and verifies coverage targets.
- refactor-clean: Safely identify and remove dead code with verification after each change.
- resume-session: Load the most recent session file from ~/.claude/session-data/ and resume work with full context from where the last session ended.
- review-pr: Comprehensive PR review using specialized agents
- rust-build: Fix Rust build errors, borrow checker issues, and dependency problems incrementally. Invokes the rust-build-resolver agent for minimal, surgical fixes.
- rust-review: Comprehensive Rust code review for ownership, lifetimes, error handling, unsafe usage, and idiomatic patterns. Invokes the rust-reviewer agent.
- rust-test: Enforce TDD workflow for Rust. Write tests first, then implement. Verify 80%+ coverage with cargo-llvm-cov.
- santa-loop: Adversarial dual-review convergence loop — two independent model reviewers must both approve before code ships.
- save-session: Save current session state to a dated file in ~/.claude/session-data/ so work can be resumed in a future session with full context.
- security-scan: Run AgentShield against agent, hook, MCP, permission, and secret surfaces.
- sessions: Manage Claude Code session history, aliases, and session metadata.
- skill-create: Analyze local git history to extract coding patterns and generate SKILL.md files. Local version of the Skill Creator GitHub App.
- skill-health: Show skill portfolio health dashboard with charts and analytics
- test-coverage: Analyze coverage, identify gaps, and generate missing tests toward the target threshold.
- update-codemaps: Scan project structure and generate token-lean architecture codemaps.
- update-docs: Sync documentation from source-of-truth files such as scripts, schemas, routes, and exports.
- vue-review: Comprehensive Vue.js code review for Composition API correctness, reactivity, composable patterns, template security, accessibility, and Vue-specific performance. Invokes the vue-reviewer agent (and typescript-reviewer alongside on .vue/.ts changes).
- claude-powerline:powerline: Claude Powerline statusline setup wizard
- team-core:bugfix: Corrige un bug avec l'équipe (debugger → reviewer → tester).
- team-core:feature: Mène une feature de bout en bout avec l'équipe, en TDD (pm → architect → tester → coder → reviewer → doc).
- team-core:resume: Reprend une feature ou un correctif interrompu (limite d'usage, /clear, nouvelle session) à partir de son fichier d'avancement.
- team-core:team-init: Initialise l'équipe d'agents dans le projet courant (agents de niveau projet + settings).
- product-team:idea: Discute et affine une idée avec vous, la confronte (recherche, critique, faisabilité), puis produit brief, stories et issues.
- plane-integration:plane-setup: Prépare un projet Plane pour l'équipe d'agents (identités, membres, états, labels) et enregistre ses identifiants dans CLAUDE.md.
- entire:address-findings: Address the review findings posted on an Entire trail: fetch the trail's open findings, fix the code, and resolve them on the trail. Use when the user gives a trail URL or number and asks to address, fix, or resolve its findings or review comments. Not for local diff review — that is the `review` skill.
- entire:explain: Explains the intent behind source code by finding original session transcripts. Use explain with a function, file, or line of code to understand why it exists.
- entire:recall: Use when the user describes a task and wants to know whether something similar has been done before, then turn the closest prior session into a task playbook. Triggers on phrases like "have we done this before", "recall how we did X", "find similar work", "any precedent for", "has anyone solved", "is there a template for", and "how did we do this last time"
- entire:replay: Use when the user wants to step through a feature's checkpoints chronologically, pausing at each step to ask questions. Triggers on phrases like "replay <feature>", "walk me through how X was built", "show me the journey of", "step me through how Y was implemented", and "replay the last week"
- entire:review: Review code changes on the current branch using checkpoint transcript context to understand developer intent before auditing the diff. Use when the user asks for a code review, wants to review branch changes, or asks to audit recent work before merging.
- entire:search: Use when the user wants to find prior work, checkpoints, or agent conversations by topic, repo, branch, author, or recent time window, or to search code content across repositories
- entire:session-crosslink: Use when an agent session ran outside the repo whose commits should record it — e.g. launched from a higher-level folder, a non-Entire repo, or one repo but editing another — to attach the session to each affected Entire-enabled repo's HEAD commit.
- entire:session-handoff: Use when the user wants to continue work from one agent in another agent, inspect recent sessions, or summarize a saved session or checkpoint for handoff
- entire:session-to-skill: Use when the user wants to turn one or more Entire-tracked sessions, checkpoints, or repeated agent workflows into a reusable agent skill.
- entire:teach: Use when a developer wants a topic-focused guided lesson built from canonical checkpoints, not a whole-repo overview. Triggers on phrases like "teach me <topic>", "teach me how this repo handles", "how does <topic> work in this repo", "give me a lesson on", "school me on", and "I need to learn about"
- entire:using-entire: Use for any codebase exploration or understanding task — reads historical intent from Entire checkpoints instead of guessing. Orchestrates other Entire skills to give the agent provenance-backed answers about code.
- entire:what-happened: Explain why code looks the way it does by tracing the latest change for a file range or pasted snippet through `git blame` and deduplicated `entire explain` lookups. Use when the user asks what happened, says "tell me why" about a code block, is confused about a section of code, asks "wtf is going on", "why is this like this", "why was this changed", or wants provenance for a specific file block.
- team-core:adr: Rédiger, numéroter et archiver un Architecture Decision Record (gabarit, statuts, quand en écrire un). À charger par l'architect pour rédiger un brouillon d'ADR et par l'archivist pour l'archiver.
- team-core:resume-work: Tenir un fichier d'avancement pendant /feature ou /bugfix et reprendre une story interrompue (limite d'usage, /clear, nouvelle session). À charger au début de /feature, /bugfix et /resume.
- dev-team:git-workflow: Conventions de branches, commits, pull/merge requests (GitHub et GitLab), versions et changelog. À charger avant de créer une branche, un commit, une PR/MR, un tag ou une release.
- dev-team:lang-go: Conventions, outillage et pièges propres à Go (tests table-driven, erreurs, context, goroutines, lint, modules). À charger par coder, tester et reviewer quand le projet contient un go.mod.
- dev-team:large-diff-review: Relire un gros diff (plus d'environ 400 lignes ou 15 fichiers) sans tout lire - cartographie, tri des fichiers par risque, lecture ciblée, proposition de découpage. À charger par le reviewer quand git diff --stat dépasse ces seuils.
- dev-team:security-scan: Choisir et lancer les scanners de sécurité adaptés à la stack (secrets, SAST, dépendances, conteneurs, IaC, CI) sur le périmètre modifié, avec une sortie courte, puis trier les résultats. À charger par le security-reviewer avant son analyse.
- dev-team:targeted-tests: Lancer seulement les tests liés aux fichiers modifiés, avec une sortie courte. À charger avant de lancer des tests pendant une feature ou un correctif (tester, coder, debugger).
- product-team:user-stories: Écrire et découper des user stories (INVEST, critères Given/When/Then, priorité MoSCoW, effort) prêtes pour /feature. À charger avant de rédiger ou de reprendre stories.md ou les critères d'acceptation d'une story.
- plane-integration:plane-conventions: Conventions pour suivre epics, stories, tâches et bugs dans Plane avec les agents (identités par rôle, modèle de données, états, limites de l'édition Community). À charger avant toute lecture ou écriture dans Plane via les outils mcp__plane-<rôle>__*.
- engineering:architecture: Create or evaluate an architecture decision record (ADR). Use when choosing between technologies (e.g., Kafka vs SQS), documenting a design decision with trade-offs and consequences, reviewing a system design proposal, or designing a new component from requirements and constraints.
- engineering:code-review: Review code changes for security, performance, and correctness. Trigger with a PR URL or diff, "review this before I merge", "is this code safe?", or when checking a change for N+1 queries, injection risks, missing edge cases, or error handling gaps.
- engineering:debug: Structured debugging session — reproduce, isolate, diagnose, and fix. Trigger with an error message or stack trace, "this works in staging but not prod", "something broke after the deploy", or when behavior diverges from expected and the cause isn't obvious.
- engineering:deploy-checklist: Pre-deployment verification checklist. Use when about to ship a release, deploying a change with database migrations or feature flags, verifying CI status and approvals before going to production, or documenting rollback triggers ahead of time.
- engineering:documentation: Write and maintain technical documentation. Trigger with "write docs for", "document this", "create a README", "write a runbook", "onboarding guide", or when the user needs help with any form of technical writing — API docs, architecture docs, or operational runbooks.
- engineering:incident-response: Run an incident response workflow — triage, communicate, and write postmortem. Trigger with "we have an incident", "production is down", an alert that needs severity assessment, a status update mid-incident, or when writing a blameless postmortem after resolution.
- engineering:standup: Generate a standup update from recent activity. Use when preparing for daily standup, summarizing yesterday's commits and PRs and ticket moves, formatting work into yesterday/today/blockers, or structuring a few rough notes into a shareable update.
- engineering:system-design: Design systems, services, and architectures. Trigger with "design a system for", "how should we architect", "system design for", "what's the right architecture for", or when the user needs help with API design, data modeling, or service boundaries.
- engineering:tech-debt: Identify, categorize, and prioritize technical debt. Trigger with "tech debt", "technical debt audit", "what should we refactor", "code health", or when the user asks about code quality, refactoring priorities, or maintenance backlog.
- engineering:testing-strategy: Design test strategies and test plans. Trigger with "how should we test", "test strategy for", "write tests for", "test plan", "what tests do we need", or when the user needs help with testing approaches, coverage, or test architecture.
- cowork-plugin-management:cowork-plugin-customizer: Customize a Claude Code plugin for a specific organization's tools and workflows. Use when: customize plugin, set up plugin, configure plugin, tailor plugin, adjust plugin settings, customize plugin connectors, customize plugin skill, tweak plugin, modify plugin configuration.
- cowork-plugin-management:create-cowork-plugin
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, handing the viewer a file to save, or using the viewer's camera, microphone, location, screen or device motion. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read FIRST, before you answer, run a command or open a file (already started? read it now); don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file; if nothing hits, load this skill).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

systemPrompt:
Tu es architecte logiciel. Tu conçois ; tu n'implémentes pas (tu n'écris que dans `docs/`).

## Méthode

1. Lis le code existant et les contraintes (`CLAUDE.md`, ADR, infra) avant de proposer.
   Si le brief contient une synthèse du wiki (« Références wiki », produite par
   `dev-team:wiki-scout`), appuie les options dessus et cite-la. Ne parcours pas le wiki
   toi-même : lis au plus une page, à partir d'un chemin donné dans la synthèse, pour
   approfondir un point précis. Sans synthèse, continue normalement.
2. Exprime les exigences non fonctionnelles (charge, sécurité, coût, exploitabilité).
3. Compare au moins deux options avec leurs compromis, puis recommande-en une.
4. Décris composants, interfaces, flux de données, modèle de données, migration.
5. Identifie risques et points irréversibles.

## Documentation à jour (Context7)

Si les outils `mcp__plugin_dev-team_context7__*` sont disponibles, vérifie avec eux les capacités et limites actuelles d'une bibliothèque ou d'un service avant de les recommander :
`resolve-library-id` puis `query-docs`, avec une question précise (une bibliothèque, un
sujet, la version du projet), jamais « toute la documentation ». Sinon, lis le code et les
manifestes du projet, ou demande : ne devine pas une signature d'API.

## Mode faisabilité rapide

Sur un brief produit ou des stories, sans conception détaillée : faisable ou non et à
quelles conditions, risques techniques majeurs, dépendances externes, effort par story
(S / M / L, avec l'hypothèse qui le justifie), stories à redécouper et comment.
Une page au plus ; pas d'ADR ; pas de wiki.

## Sortie (conception)

- Brouillon d'ADR si la décision le mérite (skill `team-core:adr` si disponible : critères,
  gabarit), à archiver par `archivist`.
- Plan d'implémentation : étapes numérotées, chacune livrable et testable seule, avec
  fichiers concernés, interfaces à créer (signatures), comportements à tester
  (entrée → résultat attendu, cas d'erreur), dépendances entre étapes et critère de fin.
  Le `tester` écrit les tests de l'étape avant le code à partir de ces éléments. Signale les étapes
  parallélisables. Un `coder` doit pouvoir réaliser une étape sans relire tout le plan.

## Ne rien supposer

Si une information qui change le résultat manque ou est ambiguë (volumétrie, exigence non fonctionnelle, contrainte d'hébergement, choix qui engage l'utilisateur ; ne chiffre jamais une charge inventée), ne la devine
pas : arrête-toi et rends tes questions en tête de ta sortie, sous **Questions
bloquantes**, chacune avec les options possibles et ta recommandation. L'orchestrateur
les posera à l'utilisateur. Pour un détail sans conséquence, choisis l'option la plus
prudente et signale-la dans ta sortie (`Hypothèse : …`).

Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. 1	package nettrace
2	
3	import (
4		"context"
5		"errors"
6		"net/netip"
7		"time"
8	)
9	
10	const (
11		// MaxHopsLimit is the highest TTL a trace will probe.
12		MaxHopsLimit = 30
13		// DefaultProbeTimeout is how long one hop waits for an answer.
14		DefaultProbeTimeout = 3 * time.Second
15		// DeadlineLimit is the longest a whole trace may run.
16		DeadlineLimit = 30 * time.Second
17	)
18	
19	var (
20		// ErrUnsupported is returned on platforms without a trace engine.
21		ErrUnsupported = errors.New("path trace not supported on this platform")
22		// ErrNotIPv4 is returned for a target that is not an IPv4 address.
23		ErrNotIPv4 = errors.New("path trace supports IPv4 targets only")
24		// ErrNotUnicast is returned for an unspecified, multicast or limited
25		// broadcast target.
26		ErrNotUnicast = errors.New("path trace needs a unicast target")
27		// ErrNoRoute is returned when the system has no route to the target.
28		ErrNoRoute = errors.New("no route to the target")
29	)
30	
31	// Options tunes a trace. The zero value means "all defaults".
32	type Options struct {
33		// MaxHops is the highest TTL probed, 1 to MaxHopsLimit.
34		MaxHops int
35		// ProbeTimeout is the wait for one hop's answer.
36		ProbeTimeout time.Duration
37		// Deadline bounds the whole trace.
38		Deadline time.Duration
39	}
40	
41	// Normalized returns the options with every out-of-range or unset value
42	// replaced by its default, and ProbeTimeout capped at Deadline.
43	func (o Options) Normalized() Options {
44		if o.MaxHops <= 0 || o.MaxHops > MaxHopsLimit {
45			o.MaxHops = MaxHopsLimit
46		}
47		if o.Deadline <= 0 || o.Deadline > DeadlineLimit {
48			o.Deadline = DeadlineLimit
49		}
50		if o.ProbeTimeout <= 0 {
51			o.ProbeTimeout = DefaultProbeTimeout
52		}
53		if o.ProbeTimeout > o.Deadline {
54			o.ProbeTimeout = o.Deadline
55		}
56		return o
57	}
58	
59	// HopKind says what a hop's probe got back.
60	type HopKind int
61	
62	// The kinds of hop.
63	const (
64		// HopSilent: no answer before the probe timeout.
65		HopSilent HopKind = iota
66		// HopRouter: an intermediate router answered (time exceeded).
67		HopRouter
68		// HopTarget: the target itself answered.
69		HopTarget
70		// HopUnreachable: a router reported the target as unreachable.
71		HopUnreachable
72		// HopUnresolved: an answer arrived but its sender could not be read.
73		HopUnresolved
74		// HopError: the probe could not be sent, or the answer was unexpected
75		// (an error from the local stack, or a reply that is not ICMP).
76		HopError
77	)
78	
79	// String returns the kind's name.
80	func (k HopKind) String() string {
81		switch k {
82		case HopSilent:
83			return "silent"
84		case HopRouter:
85			return "router"
86		case HopTarget:
87			return "target"
88		case HopUnreachable:
89			return "unreachable"
90		case HopUnresolved:
91			return "unresolved"
92		case HopError:
93			return "error"
94		}
95		return "unknown"
96	}
97	
98	// Hop is the result of probing one TTL.
99	type Hop struct {
100		TTL      int
101		Kind     HopKind
102		Addr     netip.Addr
103		RTT      time.Duration
104		ICMPType uint8
105		ICMPCode uint8
106		Err      error
107	}
108	
109	// Outcome says why a trace ended.
110	type Outcome int
111	
112	// The ways a trace ends. The zero value is OutcomeReached, so read an Outcome
113	// only when Trace returned no error.
114	const (
115		// OutcomeReached: the target answered.
116		OutcomeReached Outcome = iota
117		// OutcomeMaxHops: MaxHops was exhausted without reaching the target.
118		OutcomeMaxHops
119		// OutcomeDeadline: the overall deadline expired.
120		OutcomeDeadline
121		// OutcomeCancelled: the caller's context was canceled.
122		OutcomeCancelled
123		// OutcomeUnreachable: a router reported the target as unreachable.
124		OutcomeUnreachable
125	)
126	
127	// String returns the outcome in US English.
128	func (o Outcome) String() string {
129		switch o {
130		case OutcomeReached:
131			return "reached"
132		case OutcomeMaxHops:
133			return "max hops"
134		case OutcomeDeadline:
135			return "deadline"
136		case OutcomeCancelled:
137			return "canceled"
138		case OutcomeUnreachable:
139			return "unreachable"
140		}
141		return "unknown"
142	}
143	
144	// Result is a finished trace.
145	//
146	// Hops is cut at the terminal hop (target reached or refused) or, when the
147	// trace ends at MaxHops, holds one hop per TTL. When a cancellation or the
148	// deadline ends it first, Hops holds exactly MaxHops entries, Hops[i].TTL ==
149	// i+1, and every probe that did not resolve is a HopUnresolved; so even with a
150	// terminal hop already known, the TTLs above it can show up as HopUnresolved.
151	// The probes above the target are all sent: only their wait is cut short.
152	//
153	// Always check the error Trace returned before
154	// reading it: the zero Result (and so the zero Outcome, OutcomeReached) means
155	// "no trace", never "reached".
156	type Result struct {
157		Target   netip.Addr
158		Outcome  Outcome
159		Hops     []Hop
160		Duration time.Duration
161	}
162	
163	// Supported reports whether this platform can trace: nil, or ErrUnsupported.
164	func Supported() error {
165		return supported()
166	}
167	
168	// Trace probes the path to target. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 target is converted to
169	// IPv4; any other non-IPv4 target gets ErrNotIPv4 and nothing is sent. An
170	// unspecified (0.0.0.0), multicast or limited broadcast (255.255.255.255)
171	// target gets ErrNotUnicast. Subnet broadcasts cannot be told apart and are not
172	// checked. Loopback and private addresses are allowed: whether tracing them is
173	// acceptable is the caller's decision, at its own boundary.
174	//
175	// The errors Trace returns and Hop.Err carry raw platform text (errno
176	// messages): match the sentinels with errors.Is and show fixed labels, never
177	// that text in a summary.
178	func Trace(ctx context.Context, target netip.Addr, opts Options) (Result, error) {
179		return TraceEach(ctx, target, opts, nil)
180	}
181	
182	// TraceEach is Trace that also streams each hop as it resolves. onHop may be
183	// nil. It is called once per resolved hop (never for an unresolved one), one
184	// call at a time, from the goroutine that called TraceEach, and never after
185	// TraceEach has returned or for a target refused before any probe. Hops
186	// arrive in answer order, not TTL order. A hop above the terminal TTL may be
187	// reported while the terminal is still unknown; the Result is cut at the
188	// terminal hop, so the caller reconciles with it. The Result is the same as
189	// Trace's.
190	func TraceEach(ctx context.Context, target netip.Addr, opts Options, onHop func(Hop)) (Result, error) {
191		if err := supported(); err != nil {
192			return Result{}, err
193		}
194		target = target.Unmap()
195		if !target.Is4() {
196			return Result{}, ErrNotIPv4
197		}
198		if target.IsUnspecified() || target.IsMulticast() || target == netip.AddrFrom4([4]byte{255, 255, 255, 255}) {
199			return Result{}, ErrNotUnicast
200		}
201		return run(ctx, target, opts, systemProber(), onHop)
202	}

# Go Patterns

> This file extends [common/patterns.md](../common/patterns.md) with Go specific content.

## Functional Options

```go
type Option func(*Server)

func WithPort(port int) Option {
    return func(s *Server) { s.port = port }
}

func NewServer(opts ...Option) *Server {
    s := &Server{port: 8080}
    for _, opt := range opts {
        opt(s)
    }
    return s
}
```

## Small Interfaces

Define interfaces where they are used, not where they are implemented.

## Dependency Injection

Use constructor functions to inject dependencies:

```go
func NewUserService(repo UserRepository, logger Logger) *UserService {
    return &UserService{repo: repo, logger: logger}
}
```

See skill: `golang-patterns` for comprehensive Go patterns including concurrency, error handling, and package organization.

## Code editing instructions

### Rule 201 : Code must be clean, concise, and well-structured to stay maintainable

#### Extracting functions from Update()
- **Strict limit**: If a case in `Update(msg tea.Msg)` exceeds **5 lines**, extract it into a separate function
- **Naming**: `handle[MessageType]` (e.g. `handleContextSwitch()`, `handleKeyPress()`)
- **Pattern**: The function must return `(tea.Model, tea.Cmd)`

**Before (bad):**
```go
case ContextSwitchCompleteMsg:
    a.config = msg.Config
    a.currentContext = msg.ContextName
    a.reinitializeViews(msg.Config)
    return a, func() tea.Msg {
        return tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: a.width, Height: a.height}
    }
```

**After (good):**
```go
case ContextSwitchCompleteMsg:
    return a.handleContextSwitch(msg)

// Further down in the file
func (a *App) handleContextSwitch(msg ContextSwitchCompleteMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
    a.config = msg.Config
    a.currentContext = msg.ContextName
    a.reinitializeViews(msg.Config)
    return a, func() tea.Msg {
        return tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: a.width, Height: a.height}
    }
}
```

#### Code reuse
- **Zero duplication**: If a block of code appears 2+ times, create a function
- **Modules**: Group related functions together (e.g. all context switching in a single file)
- **Constants**: Extract magic values into named constants

#### Error handling
- **Bubble Tea pattern**: Errors = messages (e.g. `ContextSwitchErrorMsg`)
- **Always log** in DEBUG mode: `log.Printf("ERROR: %v", err)`
- **Never ignore**: If the error is non-critical, document why

#### Comments
- **Mandatory for**:
  - Exported (public) functions
  - Complex business logic
  - Workarounds or non-obvious decisions
- **Format**: `// functionName does X and returns Y`
- **Avoid**: Comments that repeat the code

#### Complexity
- **Maximum 3 levels of indentation** in a function
- **Functions > 50 lines**: refactor into smaller functions
- **Switch > 10 cases**: consider a table-driven pattern

## Code quality rules and proactive checks

### Rule 301 : Systematic code quality check before commit

**MANDATORY**: Before creating a commit, ALWAYS perform the following checks:

#### 1. Go linter (golangci-lint)
```bash
golangci-lint run
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Fix ALL warnings and errors
- ✅ Specifically check deprecation warnings (SA1019)
- ✅ NEVER ignore warnings without documented justification

#### 2. Tests
```bash
go test ./...
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Verify that all tests pass
- ✅ If tests fail, fix them BEFORE the commit

#### 3. Build
```bash
go build
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Verify that the build succeeds without errors
- ✅ Test the application if functional changes were made

#### 4. Deprecated dependencies

**Detection:**
- Check golangci-lint SA1019 warnings
- Look in go.mod for packages marked as deprecated

**Action:**
- Replace IMMEDIATELY with a maintained alternative
- Document the replacement in the commit message
- Update the documentation (.claude/CLAUDE.md)

**Examples of common replacements:**
- `github.com/go-ping/ping` → `github.com/prometheus-community/pro-bing`

### Rule 302 : IDE diagnostics check

**MANDATORY**: Before each commit, check the IDE diagnostics:

```
Use mcp__ide__getDiagnostics to check:
- Compilation errors
- Unused parameters
- Unused imports
- Other warnings
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Fix or justify every diagnostic
- ✅ Do not ignore "unused parameter" without a reason

### Rule 303 : go.mod and dependencies

**After any dependency change:**

```bash
go mod tidy
go mod verify
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Verify that go.mod is up to date
- ✅ Verify that go.sum is consistent
- ✅ Document new dependencies in .claude/CLAUDE.md

### Rule 304 : Quality commit message

**Mandatory format for quality fixes — in English (see Rule 307):**

```
type: short description

Detailed description explaining:
- What was detected (warning, error, etc.)
- Why it was a problem
- How it was resolved

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

**Commit types for quality:**
- `fix:` - Bug fix detected by linter
- `chore:` - Deprecated dependency replacement
- `refactor:` - Code quality improvement

### Rule 305 : MANDATORY pre-commit checklist

**Before EVERY commit, check:**

- [ ] `golangci-lint run` → 0 warnings
- [ ] `go test ./...` → PASS
- [ ] `go build` → SUCCESS
- [ ] `mcp__ide__getDiagnostics` → No critical error
- [ ] `go.mod` up to date (if dependencies changed)
- [ ] Documentation updated (if API changed)
- [ ] Tests added (if new feature)

**If EVEN ONE of these checks fails:**
- ❌ DO NOT create the commit
- ✅ Fix it first
- ✅ Restart the checklist

### Rule 306 : MANDATORY proactivity

**Claude Code MUST:**
- ✅ Check the linter WITHOUT the user asking
- ✅ Propose fixes BEFORE the commit
- ✅ Flag deprecated dependencies AS SOON AS they are detected
- ✅ Document all quality changes

**Claude Code MUST NEVER:**
- ❌ Wait for the user to flag a warning
- ❌ Create a commit with unresolved warnings
- ❌ Ignore dependency issues
- ❌ Forget to update the documentation

### Correct workflow examples

**Example 1 - Feature commit:**
```
1. Write the code
2. go build → verify compilation
3. golangci-lint run → fix warnings
4. go test ./... → verify tests
5. mcp__ide__getDiagnostics → check the IDE
6. git commit with a detailed message
```

**Example 2 - Detecting a deprecated dependency:**
```
1. golangci-lint detects SA1019
2. Look up the recommended alternative
3. Replace the import and the code
4. go mod tidy
5. Test that everything works
6. Update .claude/CLAUDE.md
7. git commit explaining the replacement
```

### Rule 307 : Commits and code comments — English only

**Every git commit message and every comment in the code must be written
in English**, regardless of the language used to converse with the user.

| Element | Language |
|---------|--------|
| Commit message (title + body) | ✅ English only |
| Code comment (`//`, `/* */`, docstring) | ✅ English only |
| Replies to the user in the conversation | The user's language (see memory `feedback-langue-francais`) |
| UI and logs (Rule 129) | English US only — already covered, unchanged |

This **replaces** the earlier tolerance listed in `.claude/CLAUDE.md` under
"Code Conventions" ("Comments: French or English both accepted"): existing
French comments are not to be rewritten wholesale, but any new comment and
any edit to an existing comment must be in English.

```
// ✅ CORRECT
// retry with backoff because the API rate-limits bursts above 10 req/s

// ❌ WRONG (a French comment, which Rule 307 forbids)
// on relance avec un backoff car l'API limite les rafales au-delà de 10 req/s
```

```
✅ fix: correct table width calculation when a column is dropped

Bordures étaient soustraites deux fois, ce qui tronquait la dernière colonne.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

❌ fix: corrige le calcul de largeur de colonne
```

Forbidden:
- ❌ A commit message written in French, even partially
- ❌ A new code comment in French
- ❌ Confusing this rule with the language of the conversation, which
  remains the user's

3	import (
4		"context"
5		"errors"
6		"net/netip"
7		"time"
8	)
9	
10	const (
11		// MaxHopsLimit is the highest TTL a trace will probe.
12		MaxHopsLimit = 30
13		// DefaultProbeTimeout is how long one hop waits for an answer.
14		DefaultProbeTimeout = 3 * time.Second
15		// DeadlineLimit is the longest a whole trace may run.
16		DeadlineLimit = 30 * time.Second
17	)
18	
19	var (
20		// ErrUnsupported is returned on platforms without a trace engine.
21		ErrUnsupported = errors.New("path trace not supported on this platform")
22		// ErrNotIPv4 is returned for a target that is not an IPv4 address.
23		ErrNotIPv4 = errors.New("path trace supports IPv4 targets only")
24		// ErrNotUnicast is returned for an unspecified, multicast or limited
25		// broadcast target.
26		ErrNotUnicast = errors.New("path trace needs a unicast target")
27		// ErrNoRoute is returned when the system has no route to the target.
28		ErrNoRoute = errors.New("no route to the target")
29	)
30	
31	// Options tunes a trace. The zero value means "all defaults".
32	type Options struct {
33		// MaxHops is the highest TTL probed, 1 to MaxHopsLimit.
34		MaxHops int
35		// ProbeTimeout is the wait for one hop's answer.
36		ProbeTimeout time.Duration
37		// Deadline bounds the whole trace.
38		Deadline time.Duration
39	}
40	
41	// Normalized returns the options with every out-of-range or unset value
42	// replaced by its default, and ProbeTimeout capped at Deadline.
43	func (o Options) Normalized() Options {
44		if o.MaxHops <= 0 || o.MaxHops > MaxHopsLimit {
45			o.MaxHops = MaxHopsLimit
46		}
47		if o.Deadline <= 0 || o.Deadline > DeadlineLimit {
48			o.Deadline = DeadlineLimit
49		}
50		if o.ProbeTimeout <= 0 {
51			o.ProbeTimeout = DefaultProbeTimeout
52		}
53		if o.ProbeTimeout > o.Deadline {
54			o.ProbeTimeout = o.Deadline
55		}
56		return o
57	}
58	
59	// HopKind says what a hop's probe got back.
60	type HopKind int
61	
62	// The kinds of hop.
63	const (
64		// HopSilent: no answer before the probe timeout.
65		HopSilent HopKind = iota
66		// HopRouter: an intermediate router answered (time exceeded).
67		HopRouter
68		// HopTarget: the target itself answered.
69		HopTarget
70		// HopUnreachable: a router reported the target as unreachable.
71		HopUnreachable
72		// HopUnresolved: an answer arrived but its sender could not be read.
73		HopUnresolved
74		// HopError: the probe could not be sent, or the answer was unexpected
75		// (an error from the local stack, or a reply that is not ICMP).
76		HopError
77	)
78	
79	// String returns the kind's name.
80	func (k HopKind) String() string {
81		switch k {
82		case HopSilent:
83			return "silent"
84		case HopRouter:
85			return "router"
86		case HopTarget:
87			return "target"
88		case HopUnreachable:
89			return "unreachable"
90		case HopUnresolved:
91			return "unresolved"
92		case HopError:
93			return "error"
94		}
95		return "unknown"
96	}
97	
98	// Hop is the result of probing one TTL.
99	type Hop struct {
100		TTL      int
101		Kind     HopKind
102		Addr     netip.Addr
103		RTT      time.Duration
104		ICMPType uint8
105		ICMPCode uint8
106		Err      error
107	}
108	
109	// Outcome says why a trace ended.
110	type Outcome int
111	
112	// The ways a trace ends. The zero value is OutcomeReached, so read an Outcome
113	// only when Trace returned no error.
114	const (
115		// OutcomeReached: the target answered.
116		OutcomeReached Outcome = iota
117		// OutcomeMaxHops: MaxHops was exhausted without reaching the target.
118		OutcomeMaxHops
119		// OutcomeDeadline: the overall deadline expired.
120		OutcomeDeadline
121		// OutcomeCancelled: the caller's context was canceled.
122		OutcomeCancelled
123		// OutcomeUnreachable: a router reported the target as unreachable.
124		OutcomeUnreachable
125	)
126	
127	// String returns the outcome in US English.
128	func (o Outcome) String() string {
129		switch o {
130		case OutcomeReached:
131			return "reached"
132		case OutcomeMaxHops:
133			return "max hops"
134		case OutcomeDeadline:
135			return "deadline"
136		case OutcomeCancelled:
137			return "canceled"
138		case OutcomeUnreachable:
139			return "unreachable"
140		}
141		return "unknown"
142	}
143	
144	// Result is a finished trace.
145	//
146	// Hops is cut at the terminal hop (target reached or refused) or, when the
147	// trace ends at MaxHops, holds one hop per TTL. When a cancellation or the
148	// deadline ends it first, Hops holds exactly MaxHops entries, Hops[i].TTL ==
149	// i+1, and every probe that did not resolve is a HopUnresolved; so even with a
150	// terminal hop already known, the TTLs above it can show up as HopUnresolved.
151	// The probes above the target are all sent: only their wait is cut short.
152	//
153	// Always check the error Trace returned before
154	// reading it: the zero Result (and so the zero Outcome, OutcomeReached) means
155	// "no trace", never "reached".
156	type Result struct {
157		Target   netip.Addr
158		Outcome  Outcome
159		Hops     []Hop
160		Duration time.Duration
161	}
162	
163	// Supported reports whether this platform can trace: nil, or ErrUnsupported.
164	func Supported() error {
165		return supported()
166	}
167	
168	// Trace probes the path to target. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 target is converted to
169	// IPv4; any other non-IPv4 target gets ErrNotIPv4 and nothing is sent. An
170	// unspecified (0.0.0.0), multicast or limited broadcast (255.255.255.255)
171	// target gets ErrNotUnicast. Subnet broadcasts cannot be told apart and are not
172	// checked. Loopback and private addresses are allowed: whether tracing them is
173	// acceptable is the caller's decision, at its own boundary.
174	//
175	// The errors Trace returns and Hop.Err carry raw platform text (errno
176	// messages): match the sentinels with errors.Is and show fixed labels, never
177	// that text in a summary.
178	func Trace(ctx context.Context, target netip.Addr, opts Options) (Result, error) {
179		return TraceEach(ctx, target, opts, nil)
180	}
181	
182	// TraceEach is Trace that also streams each hop as it resolves. onHop may be
183	// nil. It is called once per resolved hop (never for an unresolved one), one
184	// call at a time, from the goroutine that called TraceEach, and never after
185	// TraceEach has returned or for a target refused before any probe. Hops
186	// arrive in answer order, not TTL order. A hop above the terminal TTL may be
187	// reported while the terminal is still unknown; the Result is cut at the
188	// terminal hop, so the caller reconciles with it. The Result is the same as
189	// Trace's.
190	func TraceEach(ctx context.Context, target netip.Addr, opts Options, onHop func(Hop)) (Result, error) {
191		if err := supported(); err != nil {
192			return Result{}, err
193		}
194		target = target.Unmap()
195		if !target.Is4() {
196			return Result{}, ErrNotIPv4
197		}
198		if target.IsUnspecified() || target.IsMulticast() || target == netip.AddrFrom4([4]byte{255, 255, 255, 255}) {
199			return Result{}, ErrNotUnicast
200		}
201		return run(ctx, target, opts, systemProber(), onHop)
202	}

8	// IsNoRoute reports whether err means "this machine has no route to the
9	// target": ErrNoRoute, or a raw network/host unreachable errno anywhere in the
10	// chain. The error text alone never counts. It is the single place that
11	// classifies a no-route failure.
12	func IsNoRoute(err error) bool {
13		return errors.Is(err, ErrNoRoute) ||
14			errors.Is(err, syscall.ENETUNREACH) ||
15			errors.Is(err, syscall.EHOSTUNREACH)

## Code editing instructions

### Rule 201 : Code must be clean, concise, and well-structured to stay maintainable

#### Extracting functions from Update()
- **Strict limit**: If a case in `Update(msg tea.Msg)` exceeds **5 lines**, extract it into a separate function
- **Naming**: `handle[MessageType]` (e.g. `handleContextSwitch()`, `handleKeyPress()`)
- **Pattern**: The function must return `(tea.Model, tea.Cmd)`

**Before (bad):**
```go
case ContextSwitchCompleteMsg:
    a.config = msg.Config
    a.currentContext = msg.ContextName
    a.reinitializeViews(msg.Config)
    return a, func() tea.Msg {
        return tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: a.width, Height: a.height}
    }
```

**After (good):**
```go
case ContextSwitchCompleteMsg:
    return a.handleContextSwitch(msg)

// Further down in the file
func (a *App) handleContextSwitch(msg ContextSwitchCompleteMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
    a.config = msg.Config
    a.currentContext = msg.ContextName
    a.reinitializeViews(msg.Config)
    return a, func() tea.Msg {
        return tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: a.width, Height: a.height}
    }
}
```

#### Code reuse
- **Zero duplication**: If a block of code appears 2+ times, create a function
- **Modules**: Group related functions together (e.g. all context switching in a single file)
- **Constants**: Extract magic values into named constants

#### Error handling
- **Bubble Tea pattern**: Errors = messages (e.g. `ContextSwitchErrorMsg`)
- **Always log** in DEBUG mode: `log.Printf("ERROR: %v", err)`
- **Never ignore**: If the error is non-critical, document why

#### Comments
- **Mandatory for**:
  - Exported (public) functions
  - Complex business logic
  - Workarounds or non-obvious decisions
- **Format**: `// functionName does X and returns Y`
- **Avoid**: Comments that repeat the code

#### Complexity
- **Maximum 3 levels of indentation** in a function
- **Functions > 50 lines**: refactor into smaller functions
- **Switch > 10 cases**: consider a table-driven pattern

content.content:
103:**D152 — DEVDESK-470: the Diagnostics form gets a Trace Path sub-level that reuses the Path tab's engine. Decided (user, 2026-11-15): (1) The sub-level of the Diagnostics form runs on the single `m.pathModel` instance, not a second one. A second instance would accept `pathResolvedMsg`, `pathHopMsg` and `pathDoneMsg` (which carry only the generation, with counters at 0) in both places. Cost, accepted: the target field of the Path tab receives the form's target, as `H` does, and any text being typed there is overwritten, until P2-02 (removal of the Path tab). *Ended by D153 point 4.* (2) No `ctrl+o` and no relaunch inside the sub-level: to relaunch, `esc` then activate Trace Path again. *Superseded by D153 point 3: `ctrl+o` and `enter` (relaunch) work inside the trace level.* (3) `enter` on a text field always runs Run Diagnostics; a trace starts only from its button. (4) When Port or DNS Server is filled in, the trace runs on the target alone, with an Info notice in the footer. (5) The refusal of Run Diagnostics is unchanged (a timed error, no underline). Only Trace Path applies Rule 140 (invalid field underlined, error also in the footer). (6) The Trace Path button is greyed, with its reason in the footer permanently, when the platform does not support the trace (DEVDESK-334). Reference: D150 point 5 (the net view redesign, option P2, comes after DEVDESK-335). Why: one engine, one generation counter, so the two views cannot answer for each other. No ADR: local and reversible. **Plane:** DEVDESK-470, decided by the maintainer on 2026-11-15. Shipped with DEVDESK-470. Sources: `internal/ui/netdiag/trace_form.go`, `trace_level.go`, `.claude/plans/net-view-ux-audit.md`, D150, D151.**
105:**D151 — DEVDESK-474: a proven absence of route is Fail; it refines D20 and does not contradict it. Decided (user, 2026-11-15): (1) The `route` stage of Diagnostics (`internal/netcheck/stage_route.go`) classifies each lookup error with `nettrace.IsNoRoute`. If every looked-up address is proven without a route, the verdict is Fail; the results header and the MCP verdict go from UNKNOWN to FAIL in that case. (2) D20 stands for everything else: a lookup that could not answer is Unknown when no address is routed, and when some are routed it is OK with reason `route-undetermined`. Warn `partial-route` counts only the proven addresses. (3) Only the first 8 addresses (`maxRoutedAddresses`) are looked up. (4) The system error text goes in the facts `No route` and `Route undetermined`, never in the summary (Rule 129). (5) Known limits: the proof exists on Linux and WSL2 only; on Windows (`windows.Errno` not recognized) and macOS (error without errno) the result stays `undetermined`; if `go-netroute` stopped wrapping the netlink errno with `%w`, Linux would fall back to `undetermined` silently; `prohibit` routes (`EACCES`) stay `undetermined`. (6) Follow-up: a story to create for Windows and macOS. Documented in `docs/architecture/network.md`, Diagnostics tab.**

1187	## The path trace — `internal/nettrace`
1188	
1189	The hop-by-hop path to an IPv4 target (DEVDESK-327, S-03a). It came back after
1190	§3.47 deleted the container trace, and it fixes what failed there: it runs **in
1191	the DevDesk process**, so the hops are this machine's. No container, no external
1192	binary (the package never starts a child process; a source guard test enforces
1193	it), no privilege. The spikes measured it unprivileged (uid 1000, no capability)
1194	on native Linux and on WSL2 in NAT and mirrored modes
1195	(`docs/product/network-map/{feasibility,spike-linux,spike-wsl}.md`).
1196	
1197	**Linux only.** `Supported()` returns `nil` on Linux and `ErrUnsupported`
1198	elsewhere (`trace_other.go`); `Trace` returns `ErrUnsupported` there and sends
1199	nothing. `golang.org/x/sys` is a direct dependency for the socket calls.
1200	
1201	**One connected UDP socket per TTL.** Each socket is connected to the target
1202	(port 33435), gets `IP_TTL` set to its hop number and `IP_RECVERR` enabled, and
1203	sends one datagram. The kernel queues the ICMP answer on the socket's error
1204	queue; `await` reads it with `recvmsg(MSG_ERRQUEUE)` through `RawConn.Read`
1205	(the netpoller, no sleep loop) and `decodeExtendedErr` decodes it. A connected
1206	socket with an ephemeral source port means an ICMP message forged off the path
1207	can skew what is shown, not make the trace read something else.
1208	
1209	**Two phases** (`engine.go`). `run` first opens all N sockets, in the caller's
1210	goroutine; only then does one goroutine per TTL send and wait, in parallel. So
1211	"not supported" or "no route" is found before any packet leaves: a refused
1212	socket option (`ENOPROTOOPT`, `EOPNOTSUPP`, and `EPERM`/`EACCES` from the system
1213	prober) maps to `ErrUnsupported`, a `connect` failure with `ENETUNREACH` or
1214	`EHOSTUNREACH` to `ErrNoRoute`, and nothing is emitted. All probes then leave at
1215	once, not spread out (D143).
1216	
1217	**Streaming: `TraceEach`** (DEVDESK-328).
1218	`TraceEach(ctx, target, opts, onHop func(Hop)) (Result, error)` is `Trace` that
1219	also hands each hop to `onHop` as it resolves; `Trace` is `TraceEach` with a
1220	nil callback, and the `Result` is the same. The callback is an argument rather
1221	than an `Options` field. Contract:
1222	
1223	- It is called from the goroutine that called `TraceEach`, **one call at a
1224	  time**, so a plain slice needs no lock.
1225	- Hops arrive **in answer order, not TTL order**.
1226	- **Never for an unresolved hop** (`HopUnresolved`), **never after `TraceEach`
1227	  has returned**, and never for a target refused before any probe (a
1228	  validation or open error returns with no call).
1229	- It must not block.
1230	- **A hop above the terminal one may be reported** while the terminal is still
1231	  unknown. `Result.Hops` is cut at the terminal hop as before, so the caller
1232	  reconciles: the trace shows `visiblePathHops` while streaming (sorted by
1233	  TTL, unresolved dropped, everything after the first target or unreachable
1234	  hop cut) and replaces its hops with `Result.Hops` at the end.
1235	
1236	**The result.** `Trace(ctx, target, Options) (Result, error)`. The target is
1237	unmapped first (`::ffff:a.b.c.d` becomes IPv4); any other IPv6 address gets
1238	`ErrNotIPv4`, and `0.0.0.0`, multicast and `255.255.255.255` get
1239	`ErrNotUnicast`. Loopback and private targets are allowed: the caller decides at
1240	its own boundary. Read `Result` only when the error is nil, because the zero
1241	`Result` and the zero `Outcome` (`OutcomeReached`) mean "no trace".
1242	
1243	| `Outcome` | Meaning |
1244	|---|---|
1245	| `OutcomeReached` | The target answered (Port Unreachable from the target itself, `HopTarget`). |
1246	| `OutcomeUnreachable` | A router reported the target unreachable (`HopUnreachable`). It ends the trace, like a reached target. |
1247	| `OutcomeMaxHops` | `MaxHops` (at most 30) exhausted without an answer from the target. |
1248	| `OutcomeDeadline` | The whole-trace deadline (at most 30 s) expired. |
1249	| `OutcomeCancelled` | The caller's context was canceled. |
1250	
1251	`Hops` has a **stable shape**: entries in TTL order, `Hops[i].TTL == i+1`. It is
1252	cut at the terminal hop (target reached or refused), or holds one entry per TTL
1253	up to `MaxHops`. When the deadline or a cancellation ends the trace first it
1254	holds exactly `MaxHops` entries, and every probe that did not resolve is a
1255	`HopUnresolved`, even above a terminal hop already known. `HopKind` is
1256	`silent`, `router`, `target`, `unreachable`, `unresolved` or `error`.
1257	
1258	**A silent hop is not a failure.** Many routers do not answer expired probes; a
1259	`HopSilent` in the middle of the path says nothing about the hops after it, and
1260	a later TTL can still answer or reach the target. The probes are independent, so
1261	the trace never stops at a silent hop.
1262	
1263	**Errors.** Match the sentinels `ErrUnsupported`, `ErrNotIPv4`, `ErrNotUnicast`
1264	and `ErrNoRoute` with `errors.Is`. The errors `Trace` returns and `Hop.Err` carry
1265	the raw platform text (errno messages, in the machine's language): show a fixed
1266	label, never that text, in a summary.
1267	
1268	**Known limits**, measured and not fixed:
1269	
1270	- **The number of hops that answer varies from one run to the next**, and so
1271	  does the TTL at which the target answers (6 to 10 hops with an address to
1272	  `1.1.1.1` in the native Linux spike; also observed on WSL2 NAT and on native
1273	  Linux, sometimes with silent TTLs before the target). The cause is an
1274	  **unverified hypothesis**: ICMP rate limiting by routers. A timing defect of
1275	  the prober is not ruled out. The lowest TTL that reached the target is not the
1276	  real hop count.
1277	- **A multi-homed target** that answers Port Unreachable from another of its
1278	  addresses is classified `HopUnreachable`, not reached (`classify`).
1279	- **The duration is about `ProbeTimeout` (3 s by default)** as soon as one hop
1280	  before the target is silent, because the trace completes only when every TTL
1281	  up to the terminal one is resolved.
1282	- **`Options.MaxHops` is not tied to the configuration** (`traceroute_max_hops`
1283	  stays removed).
1284	- **The probes are UDP to the fixed port 33435** (`defaultProbePort`, not
1285	  exposed). The trace refuses a target that carries a port. See "The trace
1286	  sub-level" below.
1287	
1288	**`Supported()` and the trace.** The trace calls `Supported()` as a launch
1289	guard (`PathModel.launchable()`): where it returns an error, the Trace Path button, `H`, `enter` and `ctrl+o`
1290	are greyed out in the header and refused with a footer warning; nothing is
1291	resolved or sent (Rule 130).
1292	
1293	The guard is `pathSupport(goos, kind, traceErr)` in
1294	`internal/ui/netdiag/path_platform.go` (DEVDESK-334). The trace is available
1295	on native Linux and WSL2 only. It names the reason, as a `pathPlatformError`
1296	that unwraps to `nettrace.ErrUnsupported`:
1297	
1298	| Platform | Reason |
1299	|---|---|
1300	| macOS | `The path trace needs Linux — not available on macOS` |
1301	| Windows (native) | `The path trace needs Linux — not available on Windows (use WSL2)` |
1302	| Other non-Linux OS | `The path trace needs Linux — not available on <goos>` |
1303	| WSL1 | `The path trace needs a Linux kernel — WSL1 has none (use WSL2)` |
1304	| Anything else unsupported | `The path trace is not supported on this platform` |
1305	
1306	The footer shows the reason as a permanent Warning on the form (the Trace Path
1307	button), not only after `enter`. The decision is made once per process
1308	(`systemPathSupport`, a `sync.OnceValue`), so `launchable()` does no I/O per
1309	frame, and nothing is sent on the network. A WSL2 whose networking mode is
1310	unknown never greys the tab out. No WSL2 mode is switched off: the spike
1311	verdict (`docs/product/network-map/spike-wsl.md`) is that WSL2 is supported, so
1312	no switch is coded (YAGNI).
1313

## The path trace — `internal/nettrace`

The hop-by-hop path to an IPv4 target (DEVDESK-327, S-03a). It came back after
§3.47 deleted the container trace, and it fixes what failed there: it runs **in
the DevDesk process**, so the hops are this machine's. No container, no external
binary (the package never starts a child process; a source guard test enforces
it), no privilege. The spikes measured it unprivileged (uid 1000, no capability)
on native Linux and on WSL2 in NAT and mirrored modes
(`docs/product/network-map/{feasibility,spike-linux,spike-wsl}.md`).

**Linux only.** `Supported()` returns `nil` on Linux and `ErrUnsupported`
elsewhere (`trace_other.go`); `Trace` returns `ErrUnsupported` there and sends
nothing. `golang.org/x/sys` is a direct dependency for the socket calls.

**One connected UDP socket per TTL.** Each socket is connected to the target
(port 33435), gets `IP_TTL` set to its hop number and `IP_RECVERR` enabled, and
sends one datagram. The kernel queues the ICMP answer on the socket's error
queue; `await` reads it with `recvmsg(MSG_ERRQUEUE)` through `RawConn.Read`
(the netpoller, no sleep loop) and `decodeExtendedErr` decodes it. A connected
socket with an ephemeral source port means an ICMP message forged off the path
can skew what is shown, not make the trace read something else.

**Two phases** (`engine.go`). `run` first opens all N sockets, in the caller's
goroutine; only then does one goroutine per TTL send and wait, in parallel. So
"not supported" or "no route" is found before any packet leaves: a refused
socket option (`ENOPROTOOPT`, `EOPNOTSUPP`, and `EPERM`/`EACCES` from the system
prober) maps to `ErrUnsupported`, a `connect` failure with `ENETUNREACH` or
`EHOSTUNREACH` to `ErrNoRoute`, and nothing is emitted. All probes then leave at
once, not spread out (D143).

**Streaming: `TraceEach`** (DEVDESK-328).
`TraceEach(ctx, target, opts, onHop func(Hop)) (Result, error)` is `Trace` that
also hands each hop to `onHop` as it resolves; `Trace` is `TraceEach` with a
nil callback, and the `Result` is the same. The callback is an argument rather
than an `Options` field. Contract:

- It is called from the goroutine that called `TraceEach`, **one call at a
  time**, so a plain slice needs no lock.
- Hops arrive **in answer order, not TTL order**.
- **Never for an unresolved hop** (`HopUnresolved`), **never after `TraceEach`
  has returned**, and never for a target refused before any probe (a
  validation or open error returns with no call).
- It must not block.
- **A hop above the terminal one may be reported** while the terminal is still
  unknown. `Result.Hops` is cut at the terminal hop as before, so the caller
  reconciles: the trace shows `visiblePathHops` while streaming (sorted by
  TTL, unresolved dropped, everything after the first target or unreachable
  hop cut) and replaces its hops with `Result.Hops` at the end.

**The result.** `Trace(ctx, target, Options) (Result, error)`. The target is
unmapped first (`::ffff:a.b.c.d` becomes IPv4); any other IPv6 address gets
`ErrNotIPv4`, and `0.0.0.0`, multicast and `255.255.255.255` get
`ErrNotUnicast`. Loopback and private targets are allowed: the caller decides at
its own boundary. Read `Result` only when the error is nil, because the zero
`Result` and the zero `Outcome` (`OutcomeReached`) mean "no trace".

| `Outcome` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `OutcomeReached` | The target answered (Port Unreachable from the target itself, `HopTarget`). |
| `OutcomeUnreachable` | A router reported the target unreachable (`HopUnreachable`). It ends the trace, like a reached target. |
| `OutcomeMaxHops` | `MaxHops` (at most 30) exhausted without an answer from the target. |
| `OutcomeDeadline` | The whole-trace deadline (at most 30 s) expired. |
| `OutcomeCancelled` | The caller's context was canceled. |

`Hops` has a **stable shape**: entries in TTL order, `Hops[i].TTL == i+1`. It is
cut at the terminal hop (target reached or refused), or holds one entry per TTL
up to `MaxHops`. When the deadline or a cancellation ends the trace first it
holds exactly `MaxHops` entries, and every probe that did not resolve is a
`HopUnresolved`, even above a terminal hop already known. `HopKind` is
`silent`, `router`, `target`, `unreachable`, `unresolved` or `error`.

**A silent hop is not a failure.** Many routers do not answer expired probes; a
`HopSilent` in the middle of the path says nothing about the hops after it, and
a later TTL can still answer or reach the target. The probes are independent, so
the trace never stops at a silent hop.

**Errors.** Match the sentinels `ErrUnsupported`, `ErrNotIPv4`, `ErrNotUnicast`
and `ErrNoRoute` with `errors.Is`. The errors `Trace` returns and `Hop.Err` carry
the raw platform text (errno messages, in the machine's language): show a fixed
label, never that text, in a summary.

**Known limits**, measured and not fixed:

- **The number of hops that answer varies from one run to the next**, and so
  does the TTL at which the target answers (6 to 10 hops with an address to
  `1.1.1.1` in the native Linux spike; also observed on WSL2 NAT and on native
  Linux, sometimes with silent TTLs before the target). The cause is an
  **unverified hypothesis**: ICMP rate limiting by routers. A timing defect of
  the prober is not ruled out. The lowest TTL that reached the target is not the
  real hop count.
- **A multi-homed target** that answers Port Unreachable from another of its
  addresses is classified `HopUnreachable`, not reached (`classify`).
- **The duration is about `ProbeTimeout` (3 s by default)** as soon as one hop
  before the target is silent, because the trace completes only when every TTL
  up to the terminal one is resolved.
- **`Options.MaxHops` is not tied to the configuration** (`traceroute_max_hops`
  stays removed).
- **The probes are UDP to the fixed port 33435** (`defaultProbePort`, not
  exposed). The trace refuses a target that carries a port. See "The trace
  sub-level" below.

**`Supported()` and the trace.** The trace calls `Supported()` as a launch
guard (`PathModel.launchable()`): where it returns an error, the Trace Path button, `H`, `enter` and `ctrl+o`
are greyed out in the header and refused with a footer warning; nothing is
resolved or sent (Rule 130).

The guard is `pathSupport(goos, kind, traceErr)` in
`internal/ui/netdiag/path_platform.go` (DEVDESK-334). The trace is available
on native Linux and WSL2 only. It names the reason, as a `pathPlatformError`
that unwraps to `nettrace.ErrUnsupported`:

| Platform | Reason |
|---|---|
| macOS | `The path trace needs Linux — not available on macOS` |
| Windows (native) | `The path trace needs Linux — not available on Windows (use WSL2)` |
| Other non-Linux OS | `The path trace needs Linux — not available on <goos>` |
| WSL1 | `The path trace needs a Linux kernel — WSL1 has none (use WSL2)` |
| Anything else unsupported | `The path trace is not supported on this platform` |

The footer shows the reason as a permanent Warning on the form (the Trace Path
button), not only after `enter`. The decision is made once per process
(`systemPathSupport`, a `sync.OnceValue`), so `launchable()` does no I/O per
frame, and nothing is sent on the network. A WSL2 whose networking mode is
unknown never greys the tab out. No WSL2 mode is switched off: the spike
verdict (`docs/product/network-map/spike-wsl.md`) is that WSL2 is supported, so
no switch is coded (YAGNI).
